notes:
Task and constraints: The input is sorted in non-decreasing order, and exactly one pair at distinct positions sums to target. The answer must use 1-based indices and constant extra space.
Idea: Start with the smallest and largest remaining values, then move one endpoint inward according to their sum.
Technique and why it applies: The two-pointer scan uses sorted order: if the sum is too large, moving the right endpoint left can reduce it; if too small, moving the left endpoint right can increase it.
Invariant: The remaining interval contains the solution, because discarded endpoints cannot participate in a valid pair after the corresponding comparison.
Edge cases: Negative values and duplicate values are supported; the unique-solution guarantee means a matching pair is returned before the pointers meet.
Complexity: O(n) time in the worst case, since each iteration moves one pointer; O(1) auxiliary space. The supplied labels are consistent.

Task and constraints: Convert a positive Excel column number into its alphabetic title, where A through Z represent 1 through 26 and later letters extend the base-26-style numbering.
Idea: Repeatedly extract one letter from the rightmost position, then reverse the collected letters.
Technique and why it applies: Subtracting one before modulo and division handles the fact that Excel letters are numbered from 1 rather than 0. The lookup list maps each remainder to A–Z.
Invariant: After each iteration, the emitted character is the current least-significant title character, and updating num removes that digit from the remaining number.
Edge cases: Values such as 1 and 26 produce one letter; 27 and 701 require multiple letters. The stated positive lower bound avoids an empty result.
Complexity: For k output letters, the loop and final reversal take O(k) time and O(k) output space; the 26-character lookup list is constant-sized. Here k is O(log columnNumber).

Task and constraints: Map a positive integer to the corresponding Excel column title using letters A through Z.
Idea: Build the title one character at a time from least significant to most significant, then reverse the character list.
Technique and why it applies: The expression (n-1) % 26 selects the letter while (n-1) // 26 removes that base-26 digit under Excel's one-based convention. A list avoids repeated immutable-string concatenation.
Invariant: Each appended character is the next rightmost character of the eventual title; after the update, n represents the unprocessed prefix.
Edge cases: n=1 yields A, n=26 yields Z, and n=27 yields AA. The input constraint excludes zero.
Complexity: If k is the title length, the loop and reverse/join are O(k) time and O(k) space. Since k grows logarithmically with n, the author’s O(log n) time label is sound, but O(1) space is not: the result list stores k characters.

Task and constraints: Return the element appearing more than half the time; the problem guarantees that such a majority element exists.
Idea: Maintain a candidate and a counter, cancelling each occurrence of a different value against one occurrence of the candidate.
Technique and why it applies: This is the Boyer–Moore majority-vote method. Because the majority occurs more often than all other values combined, pairwise cancellation cannot eliminate every occurrence of it.
Invariant: The counter tracks the excess of the current candidate among the uncancelled portion; when it reaches zero, the next value becomes the candidate.
Edge cases: A one-element array returns that element. No second verification pass is needed because existence of a majority is guaranteed.
Complexity: The single pass is O(n) time and uses O(1) auxiliary space. No author complexity labels were supplied to verify.

Task and constraints: Find the guaranteed majority element in nums, meaning the value occurring more than half of the array length.
Idea: Count all values, then ask Counter for the most common entry.
Technique and why it applies: collections.Counter builds a frequency table; most_common(1) returns the value with greatest frequency, which must be the majority under the problem guarantee.
Invariant: After counting, each table entry records the total occurrences of its key, so the largest-frequency entry is the required answer.
Edge cases: A one-element array produces one counter entry. The repeated collections imports are redundant but do not change the result when the module is available.
Complexity: Counting is O(n) expected time; selecting the most common entry is typically O(u log u) or implementation-dependent for u distinct values, and the counter uses O(u) space. This does not meet the follow-up O(1)-space target. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Return the majority value, guaranteed to occur more than half the time.
Idea: Build a frequency counter, sort all distinct values by their counts in descending order, and return the first key.
Technique and why it applies: Counter.items() provides each value and its frequency; the key function sorts by frequency, and reverse=True places the largest count first.
Invariant: Once sorting completes, the first pair has a frequency at least as large as every other pair, so its value is the majority.
Edge cases: A single distinct value yields a one-item list. The repeated imports are unnecessary but not a behavioral issue.
Complexity: Counting takes O(n) expected time and O(u) space for u distinct values; sorting the u pairs costs O(u log u), with additional O(u) storage. This is less efficient than the constant-space vote algorithm for the follow-up. No author complexity labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Find the guaranteed majority element in a nonempty array.
Idea: Run Boyer–Moore voting with a candidate and balance counter, then return the final candidate.
Technique and why it applies: Each nonmatching value cancels one candidate vote; when the balance is zero, the next item starts a new candidate group. A true majority survives these cancellations.
Invariant: The counter represents the uncancelled vote balance for result, and result is reset only when that balance was zero.
Edge cases: A one-element list returns that element. The implementation relies on the stated guarantee and does not verify the candidate with another pass; duplicate imports do not affect execution.
Complexity: One traversal gives O(n) time and the two state variables give O(1) auxiliary space. No author complexity labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Convert an uppercase Excel column title into its integer column number. The title contains only A–Z and has length from one to seven.
Idea: Read letters left to right, multiply the accumulated value by 26, and add the current letter's value from 1 to 26.
Technique and why it applies: This is positional base-26 evaluation with digits numbered 1–26 rather than 0–25. let_to_num maps each letter to its one-based digit.
Invariant: After processing each prefix, ans equals the Excel column number represented by that prefix.
Edge cases: A returns 1; AB becomes 1×26+2=28; ZY becomes 26×26+25=701. The constraints rule out empty strings and non-uppercase characters.
Complexity: For length n, the loop performs n constant-size steps, so time is O(n); the accumulator and helper use O(1) auxiliary space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Interpret a valid uppercase Excel column title as its numeric column number.
Idea: Evaluate the string from left to right as a base-26 numeral with one-based letter values.
Technique and why it applies: Multiplying result by 26 shifts the previous prefix one place; ord(s[i])-ord('A')+1 supplies the current digit from 1 to 26.
Invariant: Before each character, result is the value of the prefix already processed; afterward it is the value of that prefix extended by the new letter.
Edge cases: A maps to 1, AB to 28, and ZY to 701. The stated constraints guarantee only valid uppercase letters.
Complexity: The loop takes O(n) time for n characters and stores only a running integer, giving O(1) auxiliary space. Both author-provided complexity labels are consistent.

Task and constraints: Count the trailing zeroes in n!, for n from zero through 10,000.
Idea: Visit every integer from 2 through n and repeatedly divide it by five while it is divisible by five, counting each factor removed.
Technique and why it applies: A trailing zero comes from a factor pair 2×5; factorials contain more factors of 2 than 5, so counting factors of five determines the number of zeroes.
Invariant: res equals the total number of factors of five extracted from all integers processed so far.
Edge cases: n=0, 1, 2, 3, and 4 yield zero; 5 contributes one factor, and 25 contributes two additional factors through repeated division.
Complexity: The outer loop visits O(n) integers; the inner divisions add only the total number of extracted factors, so overall time is O(n), with O(1) auxiliary space. This is linear, not the logarithmic-time follow-up.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum starting health that permits a right/down path through the dungeon without health reaching zero or below. Grid dimensions can each be as large as 200.
Idea: Work backward from the princess, computing the minimum health needed upon entering each cell.
Technique and why it applies: For each cell, take the smaller requirement of the cell below and the cell to the right, subtract the current cell value, and clamp the result to at least one. The sentinel at (m, n-1) supplies the terminal requirement.
Invariant: dp[(i,j)] is intended to be the minimum health needed before entering cell (i,j) to survive an optimal continuation.
Edge cases: Negative rooms increase the required health; positive rooms reduce it but never make the required value less than one. The code references defaultdict and inf without importing or defining them in the shown snippet, so it raises NameError unless they are supplied externally.
Complexity: The nested grid loops take O(mn) time and the dictionary stores O(mn) states, giving O(mn) space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Arrange non-negative integers into a string that is numerically as large as possible; the result must remain a string because it can be very large.
Idea: Convert values to strings and order pairs according to which concatenation, x+y or y+x, is larger.
Technique and why it applies: The comparator compares the two possible concatenations; reversing the ascending sort places the preferred concatenation first. Joining the ordered strings constructs the answer.
Invariant: At each sorted position, the comparator ordering favors the local concatenation order that maximizes the combined decimal string.
Edge cases: Inputs consisting only of zeroes must return "0", handled by checking int(res). The constraints guarantee at least one item and non-negative values.
Complexity: For n values and maximum string length d, sorting costs O(n log n) comparisons, each involving concatenation/comparison work up to O(d); stored strings and sorting use O(nd) space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Return every length-10 DNA substring that occurs more than once in s. Each character is one of A, C, G, or T.
Idea: Slide a ten-character window across the sequence and count each substring in a dictionary, then collect keys with counts greater than one.
Technique and why it applies: Fixed-length slicing directly identifies each candidate; dictionary counts distinguish first appearances from repeats and allow the final output to be built in a second pass.
Invariant: After each window, seqs[curr] records how many times that exact ten-character substring has appeared among processed windows.
Edge cases: If s is shorter than ten characters, the loop does not run and the result is empty. A repeated substring is appended once regardless of how many times it occurs.
Complexity: There are O(n) windows and each slice/hash operation handles a fixed ten characters, so time is O(n); the dictionary and result require O(n) space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Identify repeated ten-character DNA sequences in a string over A, C, G, and T.
Idea: Encode each rolling ten-character window as a compact integer, remember first sightings, and append a substring only when its code is seen again for the first time.
Technique and why it applies: Shifting by three bits and masking with 30 bits retains the latest ten 3-bit character codes. The low three bits of the four allowed uppercase letters are distinct, so the encoding distinguishes valid windows.
Invariant: Once a full window has been processed, rolling_hash represents its ten-character suffix; a dictionary value of True means seen once, while False means its repeat was already reported.
Edge cases: The code does not explicitly wait until index 9, but the early rolling prefixes have different bit lengths and are not reported unless a code repeats. The fixed-width mask preserves ten characters.
Complexity: Each character is processed in O(1), yielding O(n) expected time and O(n) dictionary/output space. No author labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Maximize profit using at most k buy/sell transactions, with no overlapping holdings. Prices may be empty and k may be zero.
Idea: Maintain arrays for the best state after buying and after selling, indexed by transaction count.
Technique and why it applies: For each price, update buy[i] from the previous sell state minus the price, then update sell[i] from the current buy state plus the price. The arrays compact the dynamic program across days.
Invariant: buy[i] is the best balance while holding after up to i transaction stages; sell[i] is the best profit after selling within i stages.
Edge cases: k=0 returns zero through sell[-1]; an empty price list also returns zero. However, the shown code uses inf without importing or defining it, so it raises NameError unless that name exists in the surrounding environment.
Complexity: For p prices, the nested loops cost O(pk) time and the two arrays use O(k) space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Maximize stock profit with at most k transactions. The implementation uses a shortcut when k is large relative to the number of days.
Idea: If there are enough transactions to capture every upward price move, sum all positive adjacent differences; otherwise use a transaction-indexed dynamic program.
Technique and why it applies: The unlimited-transactions case accumulates each profitable rise. The bounded case updates best buy and sell balances for each transaction count on every day.
Invariant: In the DP branch, max_buy[j] and max_sell[j] store the best achievable holding balance and realized profit for the corresponding transaction allowance.
Edge cases: Empty prices return zero via the shortcut; k=0 also takes the shortcut for ordinary nonempty lists. The helper's sprices parameter is unused because it refers to the outer prices variable instead. The repeated imports are redundant.
Complexity: The DP branch is O(pk) time and O(k) space for p days; the shortcut is O(p) time and O(1) extra space. The supplied O(k*n) and O(k) labels correctly describe the general worst case.

Task and constraints: Compute maximum profit from at most k non-overlapping stock transactions. This implementation first extracts rising price intervals, then selects the largest interval profits.
Idea: Build candidate valley-to-peak intervals with a stack, merge or close overlapping intervals while preserving profit accounting, and use randomized selection to sum the top k profits.
Technique and why it applies: The monotonic stack tracks intervals that may overlap; nth_element partitions the profits around the requested rank instead of fully sorting them.
Invariant: The stack holds unresolved valley/peak intervals in the ordering described by its comments; closed intervals contribute their profit to the candidate list.
Edge cases: k greater than the number of candidates is reduced to the candidate count. For k=0, the final sum is empty; nth_element may still be called with rank -1 when candidates exist, so this path deserves direct testing.
Complexity: Interval extraction is linear, while randomized quickselect is expected O(n) but can degrade to O(n²); total expected time is O(n), worst case O(n²), and the stack plus profits use O(n) space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Maximize the amount robbed from a nonempty list of house values without selecting adjacent houses.
Idea: Keep two rolling totals: the best result before considering the current house and the best result after considering it.
Technique and why it applies: For each value i, compare robbing it plus the older total against skipping it and keeping the newer total. Shifting the two states maintains the recurrence without a full DP array.
Invariant: Before each iteration, rob1 and rob2 represent the best totals for the two preceding prefixes; temp computes the best total including the current prefix.
Edge cases: A one-house list returns its value. Zero-valued houses are harmless, and the recurrence naturally chooses zero over negative gains, though the stated inputs are non-negative.
Complexity: The single loop is O(n) time and uses O(1) auxiliary space. No author complexity labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Find the maximum sum of non-adjacent house values. The input has at least one value, and all values are non-negative.
Idea: Update two rolling dynamic-programming states as each house is processed.
Technique and why it applies: The next best total is max(last + current, now): either rob this house and use the best total two positions back, or skip it and keep the previous best.
Invariant: Before each iteration, last and now encode the best totals for the prefix ending two positions back and one position back, respectively.
Edge cases: A single house returns its value; a zero value leaves the best total unchanged. Tuple assignment updates both variables using their old values, avoiding an ordering bug.
Complexity: The algorithm visits each of n houses once, so time is O(n); it stores only two totals, so auxiliary space is O(1). The author-provided labels are correct.

Task and constraints: Count islands in a binary grid, where land connects only horizontally or vertically. The grid has at least one row and column.
Idea: Scan every cell; when an unseen land cell is found, run depth-first search and increment the island count.
Technique and why it applies: DFS explores the four-connected component. The global seen set records visited coordinates, including water reached from a land component, preventing repeated exploration.
Invariant: Before each outer scan position, every previously discovered land component has been fully traversed, so a new unseen land cell starts a new island.
Edge cases: The set is cleared before a successful return, but recursion depth can reach the size of a large component and may exceed Python's recursion limit. The global set also makes correctness depend on the method reaching its final clear.
Complexity: Each cell is visited at most once, giving O(mn) expected time and O(mn) space for seen and the DFS call stack. No labels were supplied.
